chapter_summary:
The Raspberry Pi supports several standard communication protocols that allow it to talk to a wide range of sensors, displays, and modules. The three most important are I2C, SPI, and UART.

I2C, pronounced "I-squared-C," uses two wires: SDA for data and SCL for the clock signal. Each device on the bus has a unique 7-bit address. Multiple devices can share the same two wires as long as their addresses are different. This makes I2C ideal when you have limited GPIO pins. On the Raspberry Pi, GPIO 2 is SDA and GPIO 3 is SCL. Enable I2C with `raspi-config`.

Common I2C devices include LCD displays, OLED displays, real-time clocks, temperature sensors, and the Sense HAT. To find connected devices, use `sudo i2cdetect -y 1`.

SPI, pronounced "S-P-I," uses four wires: MOSI, MISO, SCLK, and CE0. Additional devices can share MOSI, MISO, and SCLK but need their own chip select pin, such as CE1. SPI is generally faster than I2C and is used for devices such as ADCs, some displays, and radio modules. On the Raspberry Pi, MOSI is GPIO 10, MISO is GPIO 9, SCLK is GPIO 11, CE0 is GPIO 8, and CE1 is GPIO 7. Enable SPI with `raspi-config`.

UART, or Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter, is a serial communication protocol that uses two wires: TX for transmitting and RX for receiving. It is commonly used to communicate with GPS modules, GSM modems, Arduino boards, and serial consoles. On the Raspberry Pi, GPIO 14 is TX and GPIO 15 is RX. By default, these pins are used for a serial console, so you may need to disable the console in `raspi-config` before using them for your own devices.

When choosing a protocol, consider speed, pin count, and device support. I2C uses the fewest pins and supports multiple devices on a shared bus, but it is slower. SPI is faster but uses more pins. UART is simple and widely supported but requires matching baud rates and is usually point-to-point.

screens.title: I2C, SPI, and UART Communication
screens.subtitle: How your Raspberry Pi talks to sensors, displays, and serial modules

narration.text: In this chapter we’ll learn the three core ways a Raspberry Pi communicates with external hardware: I2C, SPI, and UART. Each protocol has a clear role. I2C is a two-wire shared bus ideal when you need many devices on few pins. SPI gives you high-speed transfers but needs a chip-select line per device. UART is a simple serial link for point-to-point modules like GPS or modems. You will see device examples, the Pi’s default pin mappings, how to enable each interface with the configuration tool, and practical guidance for choosing the right protocol for your project. We’ll include concrete wiring notes and a short hands-on plan: enabling I2C and SPI, reading an analog sensor via SPI, and showing the result on an I2C display. Along the way I’ll point out common pitfalls, such as address conflicts on I2C or the Pi’s serial console using the UART by default. By the end you’ll be able to pick a protocol based on speed, pin count, and device support, and you’ll know the next steps to connect and test sensors safely.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: I2C, SPI, and UART are complementary: choose by speed, pin usage, and device type.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › I2C, SPI, and UART
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

I2C, SPI, and UART Communication

Understand how the Raspberry Pi connects to sensors, displays, and serial modules, and learn which interface to use for common hardware.

In this lesson

Pin mappings, enabling with raspi-config, use cases for I2C, SPI, and UART, and a short hands-on plan to combine devices.

Visual Overview
Shared buses, chip selects, and serial links
I2C
Two wires: SDA, SCL. Multiple devices share addresses.
SPI
Four main lines plus chip-select for each device.
UART
Two-wire serial link, point-to-point communication.
Explore Key Topics
I2C Basics
Two-wire bus, device addresses, ideal for many low-pin devices.
SPI Speed
Faster transfers for ADCs and some displays, needs chip selects.
UART Uses
Simple serial for GPS, GSM, and consoles; watch the default serial console.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives focus your practice so you can use the Pi’s hardware interfaces confidently. First, you will enable and use I2C, SPI, and UART on a Raspberry Pi, which means navigating raspi-config and making simple wiring checks. Second, you will explain the differences between the three protocols: how I2C shares two lines for many devices, how SPI trades pins for speed, and how UART creates a point-to-point serial link. Third, you will connect and communicate with common I2C devices such as an OLED or a real-time clock, and you will use diagnostic commands to detect addresses. Fourth, you will use SPI for a high-speed ADC and UART for modules like a GPS receiver, including the practical step of disabling the Pi’s serial console when necessary. Each objective pairs a clear skill with why it matters in projects, so you can make hardware choices that match speed, pin limits, and device support.

screens.title: I2C Fundamentals
screens.subtitle: Two-wire shared bus with device addresses

narration.text: I2C, pronounced I-squared-C, is a two-wire communication protocol used for short-distance device communication. It uses SDA for data and SCL for the clock. Every device on the bus has a unique 7-bit address, and multiple devices can share the same two wires as long as their addresses differ. This makes I2C ideal when GPIO pins are limited and you want several sensors or small displays on the same lines. On the Raspberry Pi the typical pins are GPIO 2 for SDA and GPIO 3 for SCL. Common devices include small OLED or LCD displays, temperature sensors, real-time clocks, and modules like the Sense HAT. A common diagnostic command is the detection tool which lists active addresses on the bus so you can confirm devices are visible. A misconception is thinking I2C is suitable for very high-speed transfers; it is generally slower than SPI and optimized for simple device networks. Key practice: wire power and ground correctly, avoid address conflicts, and verify with the detection tool before attempting higher-level communication. I2C Fundamentals means two wires, sda and scl, multiple devices by address; good for many low-pin devices.. In practical terms, two-wire shared bus with device addresses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: I2C idea
keyIdea.text: Two wires, SDA and SCL, multiple devices by address; good for many low-pin devices.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › I2C Fundamentals
Definition

I2C is a two-wire shared bus

SDA carries data and SCL carries a clock. Devices have 7-bit addresses and share the lines.

Pins on Raspberry Pi
GPIO 2 = SDA, GPIO 3 = SCL
Common devices
OLED and LCD displays, temperature sensors, real-time clocks, Sense HAT.
Key Takeaway

I2C saves pins by sharing two lines; avoid address clashes and verify devices before use.

Annotated Example
How addressing works
Each device listens for its unique address; the master starts a transaction and the addressed device responds. If two devices share the same address, neither works reliably.
Diagnostic check
Use the detection command to list addresses and confirm devices are present before coding higher-level interfaces.
Common mistake
Connecting power or ground incorrectly, or assuming all modules use the same address without checking.
Pro tip
Label SDA and SCL on your wires and use short runs to reduce noise for reliable communication.

screens.title: Using i2cdetect and resolving addresses
screens.subtitle: Discovering devices and avoiding address conflicts

narration.text: A practical step when working with I2C is to detect connected devices and interpret the results. After enabling I2C, a common diagnostic command scans the bus and reports which addresses respond. Use this result to confirm every device is visible and to detect address collisions when two devices try to use the same address. The scanning output lists address slots; a populated slot indicates a responding device. If a device does not appear, re-check power, ground, and wiring for SDA and SCL. If two devices show the same address, consult the device documentation: some modules have solder jumpers or configuration pins to change the address, while others cannot be changed and will need a different bus topology. When working with multiple I2C displays or sensors, write down addresses after detection so your code opens the correct device. A misconception is trusting labels on breakout boards; always run a detection scan to be certain which address is active. Using i2cdetect and resolving addresses means scan the i2c bus to find device addresses and resolve collisions by reconfiguring or changing devices.. In practical terms, discovering devices and avoiding address conflicts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Detect & resolve
keyIdea.text: Scan the I2C bus to find device addresses and resolve collisions by reconfiguring or changing devices.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › i2cdetect & Addresses
Process

Scan, interpret, and fix

  1. Enable I2C with the configuration tool, then reboot if required to expose the bus.
  2. Run the detection utility to list responding addresses so you can confirm devices are connected.
  3. If an expected device is missing, check power, ground, SDA, and SCL wiring and try again.
  4. If two devices respond at the same address, look for hardware address jumpers or move one device to another bus or use different hardware.
Example & Takeaway
Imagine two temperature sensors on the same bus with the same fixed address. They will both try to answer and the master can’t distinguish them. The practical fix is to use a device with configurable address or place the second sensor on a different bus or module that provides address lines.
Key Takeaway

Always detect addresses after wiring and resolve collisions before coding higher-level communication.

screens.title: SPI Fundamentals
screens.subtitle: Four main wires and chip select lines

narration.text: SPI, pronounced S-P-I, is a synchronous serial protocol that uses separate wires for data and clock, typically MOSI, MISO, and SCLK, plus one chip select per device, often labeled CE0, CE1, and so on. MOSI sends data from the master to the slave, while MISO sends data from the slave to the master. SPI is generally faster than I2C and is commonly used for ADCs, certain displays, and radio modules where throughput matters. On the Raspberry Pi the default pins are MOSI on GPIO 10, MISO on GPIO 9, SCLK on GPIO 11, CE0 on GPIO 8 and CE1 on GPIO 7. Because multiple devices can share MOSI, MISO, and SCLK but require unique chip select lines, you plan wiring for the available CE pins or provide extra GPIOs as selects. A common misconception is that SPI always needs more wires; in practice you can share most lines but must allocate a select per device. Confirm wiring and enable SPI with the Pi configuration tool before using SPI devices. SPI Fundamentals means fast synchronous transfers with mosi/miso/sclk and a chip select for each device.. In practical terms, four main wires and chip select lines. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SPI idea
keyIdea.text: Fast synchronous transfers with MOSI/MISO/SCLK and a chip select for each device.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › SPI Fundamentals
Definition

SPI uses separate data lines and chip selects

MOSI carries master-to-slave data, MISO slave-to-master, SCLK is the clock, and CE lines select devices.

Pi pin mapping
MOSI = GPIO 10, MISO = GPIO 9, SCLK = GPIO 11, CE0 = GPIO 8, CE1 = GPIO 7.
Common devices
ADC chips, faster displays, and some radio or sensor modules that require higher throughput.
Comparison & Takeaway
SPI is chosen for speed. You trade extra chip select lines for higher transfer rates. Share MOSI/MISO/SCLK across devices but give each device its own CE or equivalent. If your project needs several high-bandwidth devices, plan for available CE pins or use GPIO expanders for selects.
Key Takeaway

SPI gives speed at the cost of chip-select wiring; plan selects when connecting many devices.

screens.title: Sharing SPI lines and using chip selects
screens.subtitle: How to wire multiple SPI devices correctly

narration.text: When you connect multiple SPI devices, the common approach is to share data lines and clock while giving each device its own chip-select signal. MOSI, MISO, and SCLK can typically be wired in parallel to all devices. Each device also needs a CE or chip-select input, which the master asserts to open communication with that device. On the Raspberry Pi CE0 and CE1 are provided on specific GPIO pins, and you can use additional GPIO pins if you need more selects. Always ensure only one device’s select is active at a time; otherwise multiple devices may drive MISO simultaneously and cause bus contention. Before powering up, map which GPIO will serve as each device’s CE and label them physically. Another practical point is to confirm device-specific requirements such as active-high or active-low chip select and any needed pull-ups or pull-downs. A misconception is wiring all CE lines low or tied together; that will disable device isolation and break reliable communication. Sharing SPI lines and using chip selects means share mosi/miso/sclk, but give each device a distinct chip-select and avoid simultaneous activation.. In practical terms, how to wire multiple spi devices correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SPI selects
keyIdea.text: Share MOSI/MISO/SCLK, but give each device a distinct chip-select and avoid simultaneous activation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › SPI: Chip Selects
Step-by-step
  1. Plan CE lines: choose CE0, CE1 or spare GPIOs for additional devices.
  2. Wire MOSI, MISO, and SCLK to all devices in parallel.
  3. Wire each device’s CE to a dedicated GPIO on the master and label them.
  4. Test one device at a time and confirm MISO is driven only by the active slave.
Example scenario
You have an ADC and a small display on SPI. Use CE0 for the ADC and CE1 for the display. Activate CE0 only when reading the ADC and CE1 when updating the display. If either device uses an active-low select, invert your GPIO logic accordingly in software.
Common mistake
Tying select lines together will make multiple devices respond at once and corrupt the bus.

screens.title: Enabling SPI and I2C with raspi-config
screens.subtitle: Prepare the Raspberry Pi for hardware communication

narration.text: Before you can talk to devices from user programs, enable the interfaces in the Raspberry Pi configuration tool. The usual process is to open the configuration tool, navigate to interfacing options, and enable I2C or SPI. After enabling, you may need to reboot so the kernel loads drivers and exposes the device nodes. Enabling I2C makes SDA and SCL available; enabling SPI exposes the MOSI, MISO, and SCLK lines and chip selects. For UART, be aware that the Pi often uses the TX and RX pins as a serial console by default. If you need them for a peripheral, disable the console in the same configuration tool so your device can use the UART without interference. A common troubleshooting step is to re-check the interfacing options and reboot again, then use detection or simple read commands to confirm the bus works. Keep in mind the configuration tool both toggles kernel features and documents whether a reboot is required. Enabling SPI and I2C with raspi-config means use raspi-config to enable i2c and spi and disable the serial console before using uart.. In practical terms, prepare the raspberry pi for hardware communication. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Enable interfaces
keyIdea.text: Use raspi-config to enable I2C and SPI and disable the serial console before using UART.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Enable Interfaces
Checklist
  • Open the configuration tool and select interfacing options.
  • Enable I2C to expose SDA and SCL to the system.
  • Enable SPI to expose MOSI, MISO, SCLK and CE lines.
  • If using UART for devices, disable the Pi serial console so TX/RX are free.
Why it matters
The configuration tool ensures kernel drivers and device nodes are created. If an interface is not enabled, user programs cannot access the hardware lines even if the wires are connected. Reboot when prompted and then run small detection or read tests to confirm functionality.
Key Takeaway

Enabling interfaces in software is the first step; confirm with a reboot and quick device checks before building your application.

screens.title: UART Fundamentals
screens.subtitle: Simple serial communication for point-to-point links

narration.text: UART stands for Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter and provides a simple serial link between two devices. It uses two primary lines: TX for transmit and RX for receive. The Raspberry Pi maps TX to GPIO 14 and RX to GPIO 15 by default. UART is commonly used for modules such as GPS receivers, GSM modems, Arduino boards, and the Pi’s own serial console. Because UART is asynchronous, both devices must agree on a baud rate to interpret bits correctly. A practical caveat on the Pi is that those UART pins are often routed to the serial console by default; if you need them for an external device you should disable the console in the configuration tool. UART is best used for point-to-point communication; you cannot easily connect many devices on the same two wires because each device would need a separate TX/RX pair or a multiplexer. A common misconception is treating UART as a bus like I2C; it is a pairwise link that requires matching baud rates and proper TX/RX wiring. UART Fundamentals means two-wire asynchronous serial for point-to-point modules; ensure matching baud rates and disable console if needed.. In practical terms, simple serial communication for point-to-point links. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UART idea
keyIdea.text: Two-wire asynchronous serial for point-to-point modules; ensure matching baud rates and disable console if needed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › UART Fundamentals
Definition

UART is a two-wire asynchronous serial link

TX is transmit and RX is receive. Both ends must use the same baud rate to communicate correctly.

Pi pin mapping
GPIO 14 = TX, GPIO 15 = RX. These pins may be used by the serial console by default.
Use cases & tip
UART suits GPS and modem modules and simple console connections. If connecting an Arduino or GPS, match baud rates and wire the Pi TX to the device RX and Pi RX to the device TX. Disable the console if the pins must be used exclusively by your peripheral.
Misconception
UART is not a shared bus like I2C; it creates a single link between two devices, and cannot easily support multiple devices on the same pair of wires.

screens.title: Choosing between I2C, SPI, and UART
screens.subtitle: Compare speed, pin count, and device support

narration.text: Choosing the right protocol depends on three core factors: speed, pin availability, and device type. I2C uses the fewest pins—two wires for data and clock—and supports multiple devices on the same bus via addresses. This makes it excellent for many sensors or displays when pins are limited, but it is generally slower. SPI provides much higher throughput by using separate data and clock lines and requires a chip select for each device; it is preferred for ADCs, fast displays, and modules where speed matters. UART is a point-to-point serial link using TX and RX and is widely used for GPS and cellular modems; it is simple but requires matching baud rates and does not naturally support many devices on one pair of wires. When you plan a project, list devices, note their supported interfaces, and select the protocol that balances your available pins and the performance you need. A practical example: if you must connect a display, a temperature sensor, and a clock and you’re low on pins, I2C is the preferred choice because all three can share the two-wire bus if they have unique addresses.

keyIdea.title: Protocol trade-offs
keyIdea.text: I2C saves pins, SPI gives speed, UART is simple point-to-point — choose by device needs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Protocol Comparison
I2C
Few pins, shared bus, multiple devices by address. Good for displays and many sensors when pin count is limited.
SPI
Higher speed, separate data lines, chip-select per device. Use for ADCs and fast displays.
UART
TX/RX pair for point-to-point serial. Ideal for GPS, GSM, and simple serial consoles; match baud rates.
Decision rule
List device interfaces, map required speed and available pins, and prefer I2C for many low-speed peripherals, SPI for speed, and UART for single serial modules.

screens.title: Pin mappings on the Raspberry Pi
screens.subtitle: Standard GPIO assignments for I2C, SPI, and UART

narration.text: Knowing the Pi’s standard pin assignments simplifies wiring and debugging. The canonical I2C pins are GPIO 2 for SDA and GPIO 3 for SCL. SPI lines usually reside on MOSI at GPIO 10, MISO at GPIO 9, SCLK at GPIO 11, with CE0 at GPIO 8 and CE1 at GPIO 7. UART uses GPIO 14 for TX and GPIO 15 for RX. These assignments are common defaults provided by the Pi hardware and kernel support; they allow you to wire devices consistently and refer to pin numbers in documentation or code. When wiring, power and ground remain critical: ensure correct voltage and common ground between the Pi and peripheral to avoid damage. If a device requires different pinouts or alternate functions, consult its documentation; some boards can remap pins but that goes beyond typical beginner setups. A misconception to avoid is assuming any GPIO can act as I2C or SPI by simple wiring; enabling interfaces and, in some cases, configuring alternate pin functions is required for reliable operation. Pin mappings on the Raspberry Pi means use standard gpio pins: i2c on gpio2/3, spi mosi/miso/sclk on 10/9/11 with ce on 8/7, uart on 14/15.. In practical terms, standard gpio assignments for i2c, spi, and uart. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pin map
keyIdea.text: Use standard GPIO pins: I2C on GPIO2/3, SPI MOSI/MISO/SCLK on 10/9/11 with CE on 8/7, UART on 14/15.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Pin Mapping
I2C
SDA = GPIO 2
SCL = GPIO 3
SPI
MOSI = GPIO 10
MISO = GPIO 9
SCLK = GPIO 11
CE0 = GPIO 8, CE1 = GPIO 7
UART
TX = GPIO 14
RX = GPIO 15
Practical note
Always confirm power and ground, and use the default mappings for standard tutorials. If a project requires alternate pin functions, check the device and kernel documentation before remapping.

screens.title: Hands-on: I2C OLED + SPI MCP3008 ADC
screens.subtitle: A short plan to read an analog value and display it

narration.text: Here is a concise hands-on plan that uses both I2C and SPI simultaneously. First, enable I2C and SPI in the configuration tool and reboot if requested. Next, wire the I2C OLED to SDA and SCL and power lines, and wire the MCP3008 ADC to MOSI, MISO, SCLK, and a CE pin. Confirm I2C devices are visible with the detection command and confirm SPI is enabled by testing a simple ADC read. Then write a small script that reads an analog channel from the MCP3008 and formats the value for display. Finally, send the formatted reading to the OLED over I2C. This exercise demonstrates how the Pi can use both buses at once: I2C for the display and SPI for the ADC. Common pitfalls include forgetting to enable interfaces, mis-wiring CE lines for SPI, and not sharing a common ground between the Pi and peripherals. The goal is a reliable loop that reads analog input and updates the I2C display continuously. Hands-on: I2C OLED + SPI MCP3008 ADC means enable both interfaces, wire i2c display and spi adc, detect devices, then read adc and display the value.. In practical terms, a short plan to read an analog value and display it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lab plan
keyIdea.text: Enable both interfaces, wire I2C display and SPI ADC, detect devices, then read ADC and display the value.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Hands-on Activity
Project Plan

Read analog data with MCP3008 and show it on an I2C OLED

Step 1 – Prepare
Enable I2C and SPI with the configuration tool and reboot if required, then wire power and ground to all devices.
Step 2 – Wire devices
Connect OLED to SDA (GPIO2) and SCL (GPIO3). Connect MCP3008 to MOSI, MISO, SCLK, and CE. Ensure common ground.
Step 3 – Verify
Run the I2C detection command to confirm the display and test a simple SPI read to verify the ADC returns values.
Step 4 – Integrate
Write a small loop that reads the ADC channel and updates the OLED over I2C to display the measured value.
Key Takeaway

This lab shows how the Pi can use multiple interfaces at once and teaches verification steps to avoid common wiring and configuration errors.

narration.text: Keep these core ideas front of mind as you build. I2C uses SDA and SCL and allows multiple devices to share those two wires via unique addresses, making it excellent when pins are limited. SPI uses MOSI, MISO, SCLK, and separate chip-select lines; it is generally faster and suited for ADCs and fast displays, but plan chip selects carefully. UART is a two-wire asynchronous serial link using TX and RX for point-to-point communication with devices like GPS or GSM modules; remember to match baud rates and disable the Pi’s serial console when the pins are required by a peripheral. Also remember to enable interfaces with the configuration tool before attempting device communication, and verify wiring, power, and ground as the first troubleshooting steps. These concepts guide protocol selection based on speed, pin count, and device compatibility.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: I2C saves pins, SPI gives speed, UART is point-to-point; always enable and verify before coding.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Key Concepts
I2C
SDA and SCL, multi-device via addresses.
SPI
MOSI/MISO/SCLK plus chip select per device for speed.
UART
TX and RX for point-to-point serial; match baud rates.
Final tip
Enable the appropriate interfaces with the Pi configuration tool, verify wiring and power, and test devices individually before integrating them into a larger program.

narration.text: Keep a short reference handy when working on projects. For pin mappings: remember I2C uses GPIO 2 and 3, SPI commonly uses GPIO 10, 9, and 11 with CE lines on 8 and 7, and UART uses GPIO 14 and 15. For software steps: enable the interfaces with the configuration tool and then verify devices using the detection command for I2C or a simple read for SPI and UART. As you plan, weigh speed against pin count: choose I2C for many low-pin sensors, SPI for high data rates, and UART for single serial modules. Finally, always cross-check power, ground, and wiring before running tests to protect your hardware and make debugging straightforward.
